s01.slug: TUESDAY · 9:41 AM · SANDOVAL HALL 1, ROW M
body: The fog came up off the Lagoon in the night and has stayed for class. It beads on the windshields in the Anacapa lot and on the wool of Jack’s flannel, and it smells of kelp and wet eucalyptus. Kevin’s Odyssey is nosed in by the dumpsters where it lives, and across its back glass, in white car-wash polish, it still says WHO DAT · 6 DAYS.

In his back pocket, new this week, is Gerard Manley Hopkins: *Poems and Prose*, Penguin Classics, edited by W. H. Gardner, the black spine gone gray at the creases and CARDINAL MOONEY H.S. LIBRARY — DISCARD stamped in purple ink across the edge of the pages. A quarter off the discard cart, junior spring; it rode to California in the milk crate with the rest of them. Last night *Brideshead* went on the corner of his desk, squared up and ready to go to Danny, and the Hopkins went into the pocket *Brideshead* had worn to its shape, and the Benedict holy card moved over with it, the way it moves with everything.

Sandoval Hall 1 at 9:41 is four hundred orange seats and the sound of four hundred backpacks being unzipped at once. Margot is already in Row M, all in black, oxblood Docs up on the seatback in front of her, the Moleskine open on her knee to a page she has dated in the corner and nothing else. Jack sits down beside her. The seat on his other side, the aisle seat, is empty: no OCTAVIA BOOKS tote, no highlighter, no square of black lace folded on top of a Greek grammar. Just orange plastic, flipped up.

Margot doesn’t look up. “Row M. Her seat’s empty.” “I see it.” “She has occupied that aisle at every lecture since the syllabus, highlighter in her teeth, defending it from the general public.” Margot turns to a fresh page she has no plans for. “I’m not concerned. I’m noting a departure from baseline.”

At 9:42 Adrian Hale comes out from the wings in the linen jacket with the wine on the cuff, his silver hair still wet from some emergency shower, his face the color of a man who was up very late with a bottle and believes he won. A TA hurries after him holding out the clip-on mic. Hale looks at it, and then at the TA, and the TA takes it back to the wings. He doesn’t need it. The hall goes quiet from the front rows up, like a tide going out.

“Good morning. At nine o’clock this morning the President of the United States addressed the nation’s schoolchildren on the importance of working hard and staying in school,” he says, “and several thousand American parents kept their children home in case industry is contagious.” The laugh comes up the rake in a wave. Hale doesn’t wait for the end of it. “Today: evil. Not yours. You’re eighteen; you haven’t had time.”

He gives them Hume, the *Dialogues*, Part Ten: Philo the skeptic doing the heavy lifting and enjoying it, Philo handing the job to Epicurus, Hale handing it to them from memory, one question at a time, pacing the lip of the stage. “*Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent. Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent. Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?*” He lets the last one go up into the dark at the back of the hall and stay there. Then, quieter — the first quiet thing he’s said, and four hundred people lean toward it — “The problem of evil is a bill, ladies and gentlemen. Someone always pays it, and it is never the theologian.”

Jack doesn’t write it down. He won’t need to. Under the fold-down desk the RAZR is warm in his hand. He has had her number since Saturday, off the back of Kevin’s laminated itinerary, and the cracked screen lights only at one angle, and he tips it to the angle.

choices.text: “hale is doing evil. epicurus. u wd hate it. saving u a seat”

response.text: hale is doing evil. epicurus. u wd hate it. saving u a seat

response: T9 fights him on *epicurus* and loses. He snaps the phone shut and puts it face down on his thigh. Margot has read the whole thing upside down without moving her head. “You text like a ransom note.” Onstage Hale has moved on to Leibniz and the best of all possible worlds, which he pronounces like the name of a hotel he was thrown out of. The phone stays dark through all of it.

He sends it plain. Then he sits with the phone tipped to its angle and looks at what he sent, which doesn’t take long, and goes on looking at it anyway, as if it might get longer. Margot, still not looking: “Brevity. The soul of a worried man.” Nothing comes back. Hale gets through Leibniz and starts on Voltaire, and the screen goes dark on its own.

choices.text: Don’t text. Take her notes instead, in your best Mooney cursive.
response: He puts the phone away and takes out a legal pad and writes Hume down the way the Sisters at St. Brigid’s drilled it into him, the loops closed, the capitals tall: Philo, Part Ten; Epicurus’s three questions, boxed; *a bill — never the theologian*, underlined once. By the end of the hour there are two pages, and Margot has been watching the second one fill. “You’re taking notes for two.” “I’m taking notes.” She looks at him over the black frames, pen ready, and she doesn’t write that down.

s03.slug: TUESDAY · 9:20 PM · THE ANCHOR, THE DISH PIT
s03.music: Otis Redding — “(Sittin’ On) The Dock of the Bay”
body: By 9:20 the dish pit is the whole world, and the world is steam. The Hobart slams its hood down and shakes the duckboards under his shoes; the sprayer kicks in his fist over the slop sink; racks come through the window faster than he can clear them, because Tuesday is half-price chowder and the boats are in. On the transistor over the grill a ballgame goes on low, Vin Scully telling somebody’s grandmother’s life story between pitches as if he has all night, which on the radio he does.

It’s his first shift since Monday morning — since a recorded woman said *Trumbull Correctional Institution* into a kitchen in Malibu and then his brother said *Professor* — and Jack finds he can’t look at Rudy. He looks at everything else. He looks at the Hobart’s temperature gauge and at the egg dried on the plates and at Rudy’s hands: the spatula going under a patty and over, the rosary inked around the left wrist with its beads gone soft and blue, the Louis L’Amour riding in the apron pocket with its spine taped. He knows those hands pretty well by now. He keeps his eyes off the face above them, and if Rudy has noticed, Rudy hasn’t said.

Gloria comes through the swinging door with a bus tub on her hip and the pencil through her gray bun. “Thursday we’re dark in the kitchen, hon. Hood guys, once a year. Pie and coffee up front. No dishes, no dish man.” She’s gone again before he can answer, which is how Gloria tells you things that are already true. Six hours at eight dollars is forty-eight, plus whatever the tip share comes to on a Thursday, which is next month’s book for Danny and the stamps to send it — and there’s nothing under that to land on, because the one windfall he’s had in California, a hundred of Richard Vance’s dollars, went into a swimming pool in Theo’s jeans.

Through the window he can see a slice of the front: the counter, the pie case, the two chalkboards by the register. PIE OF THE DAY: LEMON MERINGUE. JACK’S RATINGS: MARIONBERRY 4/10. Somebody at the counter feeds the jukebox, and Otis Redding comes on, and toward the end he starts whistling out over the water. Frank told him about that whistle once, in the garage, with the space heater ticking: Otis whistled the fade because he hadn’t worked out what to sing there yet and meant to come back for it, and three days later his plane went into a lake in Wisconsin, and they put the record out with the whistling in. Frank told it like it was a thing a man ought to know about the world, and then he didn’t say anything else for a while.

Rudy slides a ticket down the rail. “Slow for a Tuesday,” he says. It isn’t slow. It’s Rudy holding the door open on a conversation, the way he does about twice a shift, and Jack has a question in his mouth he can’t put down.

choices.text: “Did anybody come see you? At Soledad.”
choices.key: You asked Rudy who came to see him inside.
response: Rudy keeps turning the burger. He doesn’t look over, and that makes it easier, and Jack has the feeling Rudy knows it does. “My mother. Every other Sunday, six years. Three buses from Oxnard, and three back.” The spatula scrapes the flattop clean. “She brought Louis L’Amour, because they let you have westerns. I guess nobody ever dug a tunnel over a western.” He plates the burger and hits the bell. Then, still not looking up: “Whoever you got — write him. Even when there’s nothing to say. Especially then.”

Jack doesn’t say anything. He pulls the spray arm down and goes at the next rack as if it owes him money, and the water drums off the plates and onto his apron, and the steam comes up between the two of them like a curtain somebody had the decency to draw. Rudy goes back to his tickets.

journal.title: Rudy (the Anchor)
journal.text: Line cook. Rosary on his wrist, a ballgame on the radio, Louis L’Amour in his apron. Did six years at Soledad. His mother came every other Sunday — three buses from Oxnard. Says: write him, even when there’s nothing to say.

choices.text: “Was the Soledad dish machine meaner than the Hobart?”
response: Rudy actually stops, spatula in the air, and gives the Hobart the consideration it’s owed. “Older,” he says. “Hobart’s older.” He flips the patty. “Soledad’s was meaner.” And a laugh comes up out of him from somewhere around his belt, low and unhurried, the laugh of a man who has had a long time to find things funny.
Around eleven a paper boat of fries turns up on the steel by Jack’s station, salted, too hot to touch, on nobody’s ticket. “Dish man eats,” Rudy says, and goes back to Vin Scully.

So he keeps his head down and washes. An hour of racks: chowder bowls, coffee cups ringed brown, a platter some genius has put a cigarette out on, a high chair’s worth of Cheerios cemented to a tray. The steam does his thinking for him, which is the point of steam.

At midnight Rudy sets a plate at his station — two eggs over easy and rye toast, cut on the diagonal — and taps the steel beside it once with a knuckle. “Dish man eats first,” he says. “Soledad rule.” Jack eats standing up, over the slop sink, and it’s the best thing he’s had since Malibu, and he doesn’t say so, and Rudy doesn’t wait around to hear it.

s03b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 12:38 AM · THE ANCHOR, THE BACK BOOTH
body: At 12:38 the front of the Anchor is a trucker asleep over his coffee at the counter, the jukebox dark for once, and the back booth. Gloria pushes through the swinging door with a glass of ice water already sweating and puts it in Jack’s wet hand. “One of your professors. He comes in some nights. Take him water. Don’t take his order, he’ll give you a speech.”

Hale is alone in the back booth with the harbor black in the window behind him: the linen jacket, the wine on the cuff, a fresh glass of something brown, and a slice of lemon meringue he hasn’t touched, the meringue weeping little beads of sugar in the warm air. He has gone past drunk into precision: everything he does is slow and complete, a man setting type. He watches Jack come down the aisle in the wet apron with the water glass and identifies him in stages. “Mr. Costigan.” A pause, to enjoy it. “The spaniel washes dishes.”
He lifts his glass an inch off the Formica, an offer. Jack says he’s on till one. “Pity,” says Hale, and seems to mean it for both of them.

Then he turns his head to the window, to the black water and the one red light out on the breakwater, and says it to the glass, not to Jack, in a voice with the Oxford worn off it, something flatter and older, from farther north, coming up underneath:
*With rue my heart is laden / For golden friends I had, / For many a rose-lipt maiden / And many a lightfoot lad.*
He doesn’t go on. The red light on the breakwater blinks, and blinks.

choices.text: Finish it: “By brooks too broad for leaping / The lightfoot boys are laid…”
response: “*By brooks too broad for leaping,*” Jack says, “*the lightfoot boys are laid.*” Hale turns from the window and looks at him — all the way, for the first time tonight. “Who taught a Youngstown boy Housman, darling?” “Mooney. Junior English. Mrs. Pagliarulo.” “God bless Mrs. Pagliarulo.” Then he says the last two lines himself, quietly and exactly, to Jack this time and not the glass: “*The rose-lipt girls are sleeping / In fields where roses fade.*” He holds Jack’s eyes over the rim of his drink until, out at the counter, the trucker wakes up and asks for his check. Then he drinks. “Go home, Mr. Costigan. You’re sober and you’re boring me.”

Jack sets the water down and goes. By the time he comes back out with the bus tub the booth is empty, the meringue is untouched, and there’s a fifty folded under the plate for an eleven-dollar check. Gloria has already walked Hale out to a Marisol Yellow cab idling on the wharf in the fog. She tucks the fifty into her apron without looking at it. “He tips like he’s apologizing,” she says.

Hale laughs at that — at *home* — once, a short sound with no pleasure anywhere in it, and turns his glass a quarter turn on its napkin. “Should I.” It isn’t a question, and he doesn’t wait to see whether Jack will answer it. He drinks. “Go home, Mr. Costigan. You’re sober and you’re boring me.”

Twenty minutes later a Marisol Yellow cab is idling on the wharf with its wipers going against the fog, and Gloria is walking Hale out to it with one hand flat between his shoulder blades, the way you’d walk a tall child to the car. She comes back in holding up a fifty for an eleven-dollar check so Jack can see it through the window. “Every time,” she says. “Tips like he’s apologizing.”

Jack sets the water down on the Formica beside the pie. It leaves a ring. He turns and goes, and he is almost to the swinging door when it follows him down the aisle in the cut-glass voice again, perfectly clear, every consonant paid for: “Go home, Mr. Costigan. You’re sober and you’re boring me.”

He doesn’t go home; it’s twenty to one and there’s a rack in the Hobart. When the kitchen is clean he looks out once. The booth is empty, the meringue untouched, a fifty under the plate for an eleven-dollar check, and out the window a cab’s taillights going away up the wharf. Gloria rings it up and pockets the difference for the jar. “He tips like he’s apologizing,” she says, and shuts the drawer.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Knew my face from the Anchor before he knew my name. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing.

body: Jack carries La Flaca up the east stairwell on his shoulder at a quarter to two, the coaster brake knocking his ear on every landing and Priya’s laminate still swinging from the handlebars on its loop of yarn: BICYCLES ARE NOT RESIDENTS. He smells like the Hobart — bleach, wet bread, lemon — and three miles of Ocean Road in the fog haven’t touched it. On four, the lounge light is on.

Priya is in there alone, sitting on the arm of the couch in her Fremont High hoodie with the sleeves pulled down over her hands. No binder. No laminator. On the coffee table, on a square of paper towel, is a Safeway cupcake — yellow cake, a swirl of pink frosting gone glossy under the fluorescent tubes — with one white candle stuck in it, unlit. A mylar balloon is tied by a curl of ribbon to the back of a lounge chair, HAPPY BIRTHDAY in silver script, turning slowly in the draft from the heater: the words, then blank silver, then the words.

Priya sees him see it. “They were two for one,” she says. “The other one’s at the cross. At the Point. I tied it on before my eight a.m. orgo lab.” She says it in the RA voice, briskly, a procedure being followed. “In daylight. The rule’s about after dark.”

She meant to light the candle before midnight. Then there were duty rounds, and a girl on three locked out of her room in a towel, and by the time Priya got back up here it was midnight. “And then it wasn’t her birthday anymore,” she says, “and I couldn’t decide if that meant I still could. It’s not in the Handbook.” It’s nearly a joke; she doesn’t finish it.
Jack leans La Flaca against the wall under the whiteboard. “Whose birthday?”

“Nora Calloway.” Priya pulls the sleeves down further. “My freshman roommate. Two-twenty-two, this building — it’s a nursing major and a girl from Sacramento now. She was from Selma. Raisins. Her dad grows them. She brought me a five-pound bag after Thanksgiving, like that was a normal amount of raisins for one person to own.” Philosophy major. Soprano in the Newman choir. “She sang in the shower. Every morning. The Memorare, out loud, the whole thing, with the water running.” Priya looks at the balloon. “I’m Hindu and I know the Memorare by heart.” And then, because apparently it has to be proved, flat as a fire-safety notice: “*Remember, O most gracious Virgin Mary, that never was it known that anyone who fled to thy protection* — ” She stops. “Anyway.”

“She fell,” she says. “At the Point. Last spring — end of April.” Fast, to get it said. “Tuesday would have been twenty.” They weren’t close by then; Nora moved to Serra sophomore year. “She got busy. We drifted. That’s a thing that happens, it’s in the orientation materials.” Her voice thins and goes hard. “They said she fell. People say other things. People are disgusting.”

And then, in the voice of someone filing an incident report against herself: “It’s my fault she keeps showing up. On Facebook. I friend-requested the whole floor so I’d know your faces, and now it suggests her to all of you. People You May Know. I’ve reported it three times. You can’t make it stop.”

“It suggested her to me,” Jack says. He never clicked. He didn’t have to; he knew the name. “There’s a plate at St. Brendan’s. Under the candles, at the Marian shrine. It has her name on it.” Priya nods slowly. “I’ve never been inside,” she says. “I’m Hindu. I’d just stand there.”

It’s ten to two. Jack has been up since seven, has been sent home by a drunk professor, has a brother in a cell outside Warren who asked him to describe the ocean, and in the corner the balloon keeps turning — the words, then the silver, then the words.

choices.key: You sat with Priya on Nora’s birthday.
response: He sits on the other end of the couch, close enough to the cupcake to count as a guest. Priya looks at him as if checking his name against a roster, and then she tells him. Nora argued with Hale in office hours and came back to two-twenty-two glowing, pacing, needing to tell someone, and Priya was the someone. Nora could not fold a fitted sheet and said it was a theological problem: the corners were proof of the Fall. At every birthday on the floor she sang the harmony on “Happy Birthday,” whether anybody wanted harmony or not, and nobody did, and it was beautiful anyway.
Priya laughs — once, wet, out of nowhere — and is furious at it, and presses the hoodie cuff hard against her mouth until it goes away. The balloon turns. Jack stays where he is.

choices.key: You asked Priya how Nora fell.
response: Priya looks at him, and for a second he thinks he’s lost her back into the Handbook. “She sat on the wrong side of that wall a hundred times,” she says. “The ocean side. Legs over. Seventy feet down to the rocks, and she’d sit there with her feet hanging like it was a dock. She said it was where she went to argue.” She pulls a thread loose from the hoodie cuff and winds it around her finger until the tip goes white. “The police closed it in a week.” Flat: “Accidental. That’s the word on the form.”

choices.key: You lit Priya’s candle for Nora.
response: Jack takes the Marlboro lighter out of his flannel pocket. Candles are a violation of Residential Life policy; so, arguably, is the lighter. Priya looks at both and says nothing, which from Priya is a signed permission slip. The wick catches on the second strike. Under the fluorescent tubes the flame is small and nearly colorless, and it leans in the heater’s draft, and holds.

“Happy birthday, Nora,” Priya says, at ten to two, on the wrong day. She blows it out herself. Then she stands up, pulls the hoodie straight at the hem, and laminates herself back together in front of him. “I’m going to need you to not tell anyone about the cupcake.”

journal.title: Nora Calloway
journal.text: The name on the plaque. Priya’s freshman roommate, Delgado 222. From Selma — raisins. Sang soprano; sang the Memorare in the shower. Philosophy. Fell at the Point at the end of April. Tuesday would have been her twentieth birthday. Facebook won’t stop suggesting her.

journal.title: The Point
journal.text: A cliff, according to Priya. Nobody goes there after dark. Her rule, not the school’s. Now I know whose rule it is.

journal.title: Priya (RA)
journal.text: Laminates things. Owns an air horn. Her freshman roommate was Nora Calloway. The one rule she doesn’t laminate is for her.

s11.slug: FRIDAY · 2:30 PM · DRIFTWOOD BOOKS, MISSION STREET
body: At two on Friday the sun has burned through, and the Anacapa lot is glare and gull droppings and hot asphalt. Jack stops behind Kevin’s Odyssey because there’s no way not to. Across the back glass, in the white polish, it says WHO DAT, and then the 6 has been wiped out with a thumb, and then a 5, a 4 and a 3, each one written and each one struck through with a single hard white line, and then, big and fresh, 2 DAYS. Caught up all at once, sometime this morning, by somebody in a hurry to be current again.

Theo is leaning on the SL two spaces down with the keys hooked on one finger. “She came down at seven with the shoe polish,” he says. “In your jacket.” He was out here at seven moving the car ahead of the parking people; Theo doesn’t sleep much, and doesn’t explain it. He doesn’t ask about the jacket, either. He never asks.

The SL goes down Mission with the top down and *Brideshead* in Jack’s lap, every margin of it blank. He did it Wednesday night with a Pink Pearl, one page at a time, until his whole running fight with Evelyn Waugh lay on the desk in gray crumbs. Danny can’t have writing. Danny gets the book clean, and the notes on a separate sheet.

Driftwood smells of old paper and cat. Boethius and Mrs. Danvers are asleep on the register in one heap, and it’s impossible to say where either cat stops. The owner looks up over the reading glasses on her beaded chain, and when Jack tells her where the book is going she doesn’t blink. She ships books to prisons as the seller, “because the prisons only take books from sellers” — said like someone who has won that argument with a mailroom — and has for years, for a woman whose son is at Soledad. She slides the *Brideshead* into a mailer of her own, copies the Trumbull address off Jack’s index card in square capitals, and sets it on a scale with a brass pan. Media mail. “Two thirty-eight.” “And the mailer?” “The mailer’s on me.” He counts it out of Tuesday’s tips, two singles and change, onto the counter between the cats.

Theo comes out of the back with a book and puts it in Jack’s hands: Everyman’s Library, *Brideshead Revisited*, bound in cloth, a ribbon marker sewn into the spine, an edition made to outlast whoever reads it. He pays with a bill folded in half and doesn’t wait for change. “Not on the tab,” he says. At home the Post-it is still on the espresso machine in Theo’s neat hand, *+ 1 MALIBU —T.V.*, open. Jack doesn’t argue.

The post office is across the street, and the flag out front is at half-staff, hanging straight down in the windless afternoon. Nobody has to tell him why. Inside he buys a forty-four-cent stamp for the letter he wrote this morning at four, after he gave up on sleep.

body.title: Folded in thirds, to Trumbull
body.text:
Danny —

Describe it, you said. Okay. Sixty-six degrees. Green at the top of the waves and gray underneath. It sounds like a truck going by that never finishes going by. The fog comes in at night like it’s got somewhere to be.

I told the veil girl about you. She didn’t ask what. She asked your name.

Next month you get Hopkins. He yells at God in sonnets. You’ll like him.

—the Professor

body.title: Folded in thirds, to Trumbull
body.text:
Danny —

Describe it, you said. Okay. Sixty-six degrees. Green at the top of the waves and gray underneath. It sounds like a truck going by that never finishes going by. The fog comes in at night like it’s got somewhere to be.

Your jacket walked a girl home Thursday. Three miles. Don’t make it a thing.

Next month you get Hopkins. He yells at God in sonnets. You’ll like him.

—the Professor

body: Back in the SL, Theo doesn’t start the car. He’s looking at the flag. “Where were you?” he says. “Eight years ago.”

“Fifth grade. St. Brigid’s.” Sister Rose wheeled the TV cart in after the second plane and didn’t turn it off, and nobody did fractions that day. Jack’s mother came down from the school office and stood at the back of the room with her hand on the radiator, eight months along with Rosie. “When we got home my dad’s truck was in the driveway. Nobody sent him home from Lordstown. He just came home, at noon, and sat in the truck with the radio on. He was still sitting there at three.”

Theo nods. “My parents were still married,” he says, as if giving a date. “My father was at the Toronto film festival. They grounded everything. He and two other producers rented a Lincoln and drove home to Los Angeles. Four days.” He puts the key in the ignition and doesn’t turn it. “Longest he’s ever stayed anywhere.”

response: Theo looks at the flag a little longer, and then at the cloth book in Jack’s lap, and not at Jack. When he talks it’s short, in the voice with nothing on it. “I’m not good at much, Costigan. I’m good at not asking.” He starts the car.

choices.text: “Four days in a Lincoln with two producers. That’s a war crime.”
response: Theo laughs into the steering wheel. “He called it the best meeting he ever had,” he says. “They came out of Nebraska with two pictures and a lawsuit.” He starts the car.

choices.text: “Where were you, though? Not him. You.”
response: For a moment it looks like Theo won’t answer. Then, short: “In the kitchen. Poppy was six. I turned off the TV so she wouldn’t see.” He turns the key. “My mother turned it back on.”
He pulls out onto Mission under the flag, and neither of them looks back at it.

journal.title: Danny
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him Friday, media mail through Driftwood, margins erased; the ocean went in a letter. Lena knows. She asked his name.

journal.title: Danny
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him Friday, media mail through Driftwood, margins erased; the ocean went in a letter.

journal.title: The ledger
journal.text: Pie: paid. Bus fare: paid, with compliments. Richard Vance’s hundred: Theo’s, for the gas. A new *Brideshead*, cloth, with a ribbon: “Not on the tab.” Postage to Trumbull: $2.38, out of tips.
